images.alt: A Commodore CBM 610 business computer, a low beige case with an integrated keyboard, photographed from the front
images.caption: The CBM 610: a low-profile business machine with the keyboard built into the case, banking a megabyte of address space through a 6502-derived 6509.
images.author: Thomas Conté

images.alt: Close-up view of a Commodore CBM 610 keyboard and case badge
images.caption: A full business keyboard with a numeric pad, built for an office that would rather have bought an IBM.
images.author: Thomas Conté

images.alt: A Commodore CBM 610 business computer shown at an angle with its low-profile case
images.caption: The CBM-II line sold in the tens of thousands, not the millions, and was quietly discontinued after Jack Tramiel left Commodore.

images.alt: A Commodore CBM 610 computer photographed in a collection setting
images.caption: A megabyte of banked address space through a 1975-vintage 6502 derivative was genuinely clever engineering, aimed at a market that had already moved on.

images.alt: The rear panel of a Commodore CBM 610, showing its IEEE-488 and other connectors
images.caption: IEEE-488 on the back connected the CBM 610 to the same business drives and printers Commodore already sold — the right bus for Commodore's own peripherals, and the wrong one for everybody else's.
